201.stem:
The curves $y=e^{-2x}$ and $y=e^{-x}-\dfrac{1}{4}$ intersect at exactly one point as shown in the diagram. The point of intersection has coordinates $\left(\ln 2,\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$. (Do NOT prove this.)

\exfigure{296_q32_1}

figures.cap: curves y=e^{-2x} and y=e^{-x}-1/4 touching at (ln 2, 1/4), region shaded near y-axis

parts.latex: Show that the area bounded by the two curves and the y-axis, as shaded in the diagram, is $\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2-\dfrac{1}{8}$.
Find the values of $k$ such that the curves $y=e^{-2x}$ and $y=e^{-x}+k$ intersect at two points.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Shaded area}&=\int_0^{\ln2}\left[e^{-2x}-\left(e^{-x}-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\right]dx\\&=\int_0^{\ln2}\left(e^{-2x}-e^{-x}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x}+e^{-x}+\dfrac{1}{4}x\right]_0^{\ln2}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2\ln2}+e^{-\ln2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+1+0\right)\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\ln\left(2^{-2}\right)}+e^{\ln\left(2^{-1}\right)}+\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln2-\dfrac{1}{8}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides an antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Provides an integral expression for the area, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
We want the equation $e^{-2x}=e^{-x}+k$ to have 2 solutions.

i.e. $e^{-2x}-e^{-x}-k=0$ has 2 solutions

i.e. $\left(e^{-x}\right)^2-\left(e^{-x}\right)-k=0$ has 2 solutions.

Using the quadratic formula,
$$e^{-x}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4k}}{2}$$
For two real solutions we want $1+4k>0$, i.e. $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

But for two solutions for $e^{-x}$, both the real solutions to the quadratic must be positive.
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \sqrt{1+4k}&<1\\\therefore\ 1+4k&<1\\\therefore\ k&<0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{1}{4}<k<0$$
criteria: Uses the discriminant to find $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to form a quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{2^n-2^{n-1}}{2^{n+1}+2^n}$?

solutions.latex:
Take out the common factor $2^{n-1}$ from the numerator and $2^n$ from the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2^n - 2^{n-1}}{2^{n+1} + 2^n} &= \dfrac{2^{n-1}(2 - 1)}{2^n(2 + 1)} \\ &= \dfrac{2^{n-1}}{3\times 2^n} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3\times 2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{2^n-2^{n-1}}{2^{n+1}+2^n}$?

solutions.latex:
Take out the common factor $2^{n-1}$ from the numerator and $2^n$ from the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2^n - 2^{n-1}}{2^{n+1} + 2^n} &= \dfrac{2^{n-1}(2 - 1)}{2^n(2 + 1)} \\ &= \dfrac{2^{n-1}}{3\times 2^n} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3\times 2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

81.stem: Given the equation of a circle is: $x^2-4x+y^2+2y-4=0$.

parts.latex: Determine the centre and radius.
The line $y=mx+2$ is a tangent to the circle. Determine the values of $m$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} (x-2)^2+(y+1)^2 &= 4+2^2+1^2 \\ &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Centre $=(2,-1)$, $r=3$
criteria: Finds the centre, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For what values of $k$ does $x^2-kx+4=0$ have two distinct real roots?

solutions.latex:
Two distinct real roots require $\Delta>0$:
$$\Delta=(-k)^2-4(1)(4)=k^2-16$$
$$\begin{aligned} k^2-16&>0 \\ (k-4)(k+4)&>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k<-4 \text{ or } k>4$$

parts.latex: For which values of $k$ does the equation $x^2+(k+2)x+4=0$ have one solution?

solutions.latex:
One solution means equal roots, so the discriminant is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=(k+2)^2-4\times1\times4\\ &=k^2+4k-12 \end{aligned}$$
For equal roots, $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} k^2+4k-12&=0\\ (k+6)(k-2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=-6\text{ or }k=2$$
criteria: Uses the discriminant correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $x-\dfrac{6}{x}=1$.

solutions.latex:
Multiply both sides by $x$ ($x\ne 0$) and rearrange:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-x-6&=0 \\ (x-3)(x+2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3 \text{ or } x=-2$$

parts.latex: What is the solution to the equation $3x^2+5x-1=0$?

solutions.latex:
Using the quadratic formula with $a=3$, $b=5$, $c=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{-5\pm\sqrt{5^2-4(3)(-1)}}{2(3)}\\ &=\dfrac{-5\pm\sqrt{37}}{6}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Express $4x\sqrt{11}$ in the form of $\sqrt{a}$.

solutions.latex:
Moving $4x$ inside the square root squares it:
$$\begin{aligned} 4x\sqrt{11}&=\sqrt{(4x)^2\times 11}\\ &=\sqrt{176x^2}\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{1362_q28_1}

figures.cap: hyperbola y=f(x) with asymptotes x=1 and y=1, passing through the origin

parts.latex: Justify that the equation of $y=f(x)$ is $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x-1}$. Show full working.
Find the exact value of $m$ for which the equation $f(x)=mx$ is a tangent to $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x-1}$.

solutions.latex:
The graph has asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=1$, so it is a translation of $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-1&=\dfrac{k}{x-1}\\ y&=1+\dfrac{k}{x-1} \end{aligned}$$
The curve passes through $(0,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1+\dfrac{k}{-1}\\ k&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y&=1+\dfrac{1}{x-1}\\ &=\dfrac{x-1+1}{x-1}\\ &=\dfrac{x}{x-1} \end{aligned}$$
Checking the asymptotes:
$$\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x-1}\right)=1+0=1$$
so the horizontal asymptote is $y=1$.

The domain is $x\ne 1$, so the vertical asymptote is $x=1$.
criteria: Uses the asymptotes or a transformation of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).
meta.marker_note: Stating $x\ne 1$, $y\ne 1$ without justification is not sufficient.

solutions.latex:
The line $y=mx$ is a tangent when $\dfrac{x}{x-1}=mx$ has exactly one solution, that is, $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=mx(x-1)\\ x&=mx^2-mx\\ 0&=mx^2-mx-x\\ 0&=mx^2-(m+1)x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=\left(-(m+1)\right)^2-4\times m\times 0\\ &=(m+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\Delta=0$ when $m=-1$.

Calculus approach: the curve passes through $(0,0)$, so the tangent through the origin touches at $x=0$. Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x-1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{1(x-1)-x\cdot 1}{(x-1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{(x-1)^2}\\ m&=f'(0)=\dfrac{-1}{(-1)^2}=-1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the quadratic and discriminant (or derivative), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The quadratic equation $x^2+(m+6)x+8m=0$ has two distinct roots.

By considering the discriminant or otherwise, determine all the possible values of $m$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=(m+6)^2-4(1)(8m)\\ &=m^2+12m+36-32m\\ &=m^2-20m+36 \end{aligned}$$
For two distinct roots, $\Delta>0$:
$$\begin{aligned} m^2-20m+36&>0\\ (m-2)(m-18)&>0 \end{aligned}$$
The graph of $m^2-20m+36$ is above the axis outside its roots 2 and 18:

\exfigure{1364_q15_s1}
$$\therefore\ m<2 \text{ or } m>18$$
criteria: Substitutes correct values into the discriminant formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2}\dfrac{2-x}{1-\sqrt{x-1}}$

solutions.latex:
Rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2-x}{1-\sqrt{x-1}}\times\dfrac{1+\sqrt{x-1}}{1+\sqrt{x-1}}&=\dfrac{(2-x)\left(1+\sqrt{x-1}\right)}{1-(x-1)}\\ &=1+\sqrt{x-1}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 2}\left(1+\sqrt{x-1}\right)&=1+1\\ &=2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Giana and Maria run a painting business.

Giana paints 1 m$^2$ of a wall in $x$ minutes and Maria paints 1 m$^2$ of a wall in $y$ minutes.

Which expression represents the area of the wall they can paint in 1 hour if Giana and Maria worked together?

solutions.latex:
In 1 hour (60 minutes), Giana paints $\dfrac{60}{x}$ m$^2$ and Maria paints $\dfrac{60}{y}$ m$^2$.

Together they paint
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{60}{x}+\dfrac{60}{y}&=\dfrac{60y+60x}{xy}\\ &=60\left(\dfrac{x+y}{xy}\right) \end{aligned}$$

1463.stem: Let $C$ be the circle with equation $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$, and $\ell$ the line given by the equation $y=x+d$ for some real constant $d$.

parts.latex: Show that if $2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$, then $\ell$ intersects $C$ at exactly two points.

Let $A$ and $B$ be the two points of intersection in part (a).

It is given that the distance between $A$ and $B$ is $2\sqrt{3}$ units.

By determining the coordinates of $A$ and $B$, find a possible value of $d$, leaving your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Solve $y=x+d$ and $(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$ simultaneously. By substitution:
$$\begin{aligned} (x-1)^2+(x+d-3)^2&=9\\ (x-1)^2+\big(x+(d-3)\big)^2&=9\\ x^2-2x+1+x^2+2x(d-3)+(d-3)^2&=9\\ x^2-2x+1+x^2+2dx-6x+d^2-6d+9&=9\\ 2x^2+2dx-8x+d^2-6d+1&=0\\ 2x^2+(2d-8)x+(d^2-6d+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
This non-monic quadratic has 2 distinct real solutions if its discriminant $D>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} D&=(2d-8)^2-4(2)(d^2-6d+1)\\ &=4d^2-32d+64-8d^2+48d-8\\ &=-4d^2+16d+56 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula to find the values of $d$ when $D=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} d&=\dfrac{-16\pm\sqrt{(16)^2+4(4)(56)}}{2(-4)}\\ &=\dfrac{-16\pm\sqrt{1152}}{-8}\\ &=\dfrac{-16\pm24\sqrt{2}}{-8}\\ &=2\pm3\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
$D$ is a concave-down quadratic in $d$ with roots $2\pm3\sqrt{2}$, hence $D>0$ for
$$2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$$
$\therefore$ $\ell$ intersects $C$ at exactly two points if $2-3\sqrt{2}<d<2+3\sqrt{2}$.
criteria: Recognises that discriminant $>0$ for 2 distinct real solutions and attempts to use quadratic formula to find values of $d$, or equivalent merit
Finds an equation involving $x$ and $d$ by solving equation of $\ell$ and $C$ simultaneously, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the square of (d-3) is (d-3)^2, not (d+3)^2; the next line already expands it as d^2-6d+9.

solutions.latex:
Solving the equation from part (a) with the quadratic formula gives the $x$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$:
$$2x^2+(2d-8)x+d^2-6d+1=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_1&=\dfrac{8-2d-\sqrt{D}}{4}=2-\dfrac{d}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4}\\ x_2&=\dfrac{8-2d+\sqrt{D}}{4}=2-\dfrac{d}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Using $y=x+d$ for the corresponding $y$-coordinates:
$$\begin{aligned} y_1&=2+\dfrac{d}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4}\\ y_2&=2+\dfrac{d}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
So $x_2-x_1=y_2-y_1=\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}$. Using the distance formula with $AB=2\sqrt{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2}&=2\sqrt{3}\\ \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{D}}{2}\right)^2&=12\\ D&=24 \end{aligned}$$
Solving $-4d^2+16d+56=24$, first dividing all terms by $-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2-4d-8&=0\\ d&=2\pm2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Possible values of $d$ are $2-2\sqrt{3}$ or $2+2\sqrt{3}$.
criteria: Finds the coordinates of $A$ and $B$ in terms of $d$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Find the value of $\mu$ such that

$$n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)=\left(n^2+\mu n\right)\left(n^2+\mu n+2\right).$$

Let $n$ be an integer.

Deduce that $2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1$ is a perfect square.

solutions.latex:
Pairing the outer and inner factors:
$$\begin{aligned} n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)&=n(n+3)\times(n+1)(n+2)\\ &=\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore \mu=3$$

Let $n=2022$. Using part (a):
$$2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1=\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right)+1$$
Let $k=n^2+3n$ (an integer):
$$\begin{aligned} 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1&=k(k+2)+1\\ &=k^2+2k+1\\ &=(k+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
where $k+1$ is an integer.

$\therefore 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1$ is a perfect square.

Alternate method: let $n=2022$ and $k=n^2+3n+1$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1&=(k-1)(k+1)+1\\ &=k^2\\ &=\left(n^2+3n+1\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the expression as $\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right)+1$ with $n=2022$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The solutions to $(2x-1)(x+2)=18$ are:

solutions.latex:
Expanding and moving all terms to one side:
$$\begin{aligned}2x^2+3x-2&=18\\2x^2+3x-20&=0\\(2x-5)(x+4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{5}{2}\text{ or }x=-4$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ and $b$ if $\left(2\sqrt{3}+3\right)^2+\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}=a+b\sqrt{3}$

solutions.latex:
Rationalising the denominator with $\dfrac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2+\sqrt{3}}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(2\sqrt{3}+3\right)^2+\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{2+\sqrt{3}}{2+\sqrt{3}}\\&=12+12\sqrt{3}+9+2+\sqrt{3}\\&=23+13\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore a=23,\ b=13$$
criteria: Expands and rationalises, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which expression shows $\dfrac{45^{2-k}}{6^k}$ as a product of its prime factors in simplified form?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{45^{2-k}}{6^k} &= \dfrac{(3^2\times 5)^{2-k}}{(3\times 2)^k} \\ &= \dfrac{3^{4-2k}\times 5^{2-k}}{3^k\times 2^k} \\ &= \dfrac{3^{4-3k}\times 5^{2-k}}{2^k} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For which values of $k$ is the parabola $y=kx^2-2x+3k+2$ always positive?

solutions.latex:
Always positive requires $a>0$ (so $k>0$) and $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= b^2-4ac \\ &= (-2)^2-4k(3k+2) \\ &= -12k^2-8k+4 \\ &= -4(3k^2+2k-1) \\ &= -4(3k-1)(k+1) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{309_q10_s1}

$\Delta<0$ when $k<-1$ or $k>\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Combined with $k>0$:
$$k>\dfrac{1}{3}$$

parts.latex: If $3+\dfrac{1}{x}=\sqrt{15}$, find the exact value of $x$. Express your answer with a rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
Subtracting 3, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{x} &= \sqrt{15}-3 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{15}-3} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{15}+3}{15-9} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{15}+3}{6} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For what values of $k$ does the quadratic equation $x^2+kx-2k=0$ have real roots?

solutions.latex:
The equation has real roots when $\Delta\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=k^2-4(1)(-2k)\\&=k^2+8k\\&=k(k+8)\ge0\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}k&\le-8 &&\text{(both factors negative or zero)}\\k&\ge0 &&\text{(both factors positive or zero)}\end{aligned}$$
So $k\in(-\infty,-8]\cup[0,\infty)$, with the end points included because $\Delta=0$ gives a repeated real root.

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 7}\dfrac{x^2+5x-84}{x-7}$

solutions.latex:
Factorise and cancel $x-7$ (since $x\ne7$ in a limit):
$$\dfrac{x^2+5x-84}{x-7}=\dfrac{(x-7)(x+12)}{x-7}=x+12$$
$$\lim_{x\to7}(x+12)=19$$

parts.latex: For what values of $a$ does the equation $ax^2+5x+a=0$ have no solution?

solutions.latex:
The equation has no real solution when $\Delta<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25-4a^2&<0 \\ 4a^2&>25 &&(\text{add } 4a^2) \\ a^2&>\dfrac{25}{4} &&(\text{divide by } 4) \end{aligned}$$
So $a<-\dfrac{5}{2}$ or $a>\dfrac{5}{2}$.
